summary.text: King of the Phaeacians on Corcyra, son of Nausithous, wise in counsel by the gods' gift; he received Odysseus and sent him home with treasure, and in Apollodorus his queen Arete married Jason and Medea when the Argonauts came to the island.

story.text: When Odysseus came ashore on Scheria, Athena sent him to the house of Alcinous, upon whom depend the might and power of the Phaeacians; his daughter Nausicaa led the stranger to the city, and the king heard his tale and promised him a safe passage home.
Apollodorus names Corcyra the island of the Phaeacians, of which Alcinous was king — the haven the Argonauts reached after Thrinacia, where Arete the queen married Medea to Jason.

Homer makes him the pivot of Odysseus' last leg home: when the stranger had wept at Demodocus' songs of Troy and revealed his name at last, Alcinous promised gifts and a ship to carry him to Ithaca while he slept — the Phaeacians' final service before Poseidon punished them for aiding the man the earth-shaker hated.

When the returning ship had set Odysseus ashore on Ithaca, Poseidon asked Zeus to let him petrify the vessel and ring the Phaeacian city with a mountain — so the people who had borne the wanderer home lost their swift ships forever, and Alcinous' prayer to the god could not undo the earth-shaker's wrath.
